summary: Training volume over the last 4 weeks has been low and inconsistent, with chronically short sleep (many nights under 5–6 hours) dragging body battery well below optimal recovery levels for extended periods. Swim fitness is the primary limiter heading into the Half Oceanman 5,000m in 21 days, with only three open-water sessions logged and no pool work evident in the data. Cycling has shown reasonable aerobic effort on the longer rides (66km and 36km), but power output on the indoor sessions is modest, suggesting the bike is currently the strongest of the three disciplines relative to current form.
suggestions: Sleep is the single biggest lever available right now — body battery has been below 40 on most days and sleep duration is averaging under 6 hours; prioritise 7–8 hours nightly for the next 3 weeks to arrive at the Half Oceanman as recovered as possible.

With the Half Oceanman 5,000m swim in 21 days, pool sessions this week and next (Wk13/Wk14) are non-negotiable — focus on continuous aerobic blocks at ≤2:30/100m to build confidence at race distance, not short drill-heavy sets.

Cap the Wk13 long ride at 60km easy (as already AI-adjusted) and the Wk13 long run at 10–12km easy — the priority is arriving at the swim race fresh, not accumulating training stress that won't convert to fitness in 3 weeks.

The Wk14 threshold cycling intervals (5×5min @ 210–244W on 24 Sep) are 8 days before the Half Oceanman and should be replaced with an easy endurance spin — hard cycling at this point adds fatigue without meaningful adaptation benefit for the swim race.

Post Half Oceanman (4 Oct onwards), the Wk16 long run and interval sessions are well-timed for the Treviso 10K on 10 Oct — keep the shakeout structure already planned and trust the taper; don't add extra volume after the swim race.

proposed_changes.reason: A 20km long run today, 21 days out from the Half Oceanman, accumulates unnecessary residual fatigue without delivering adaptations that will aid the swim race; a short easy run maintains run feel without cost.

proposed_changes.reason: With only 14 days to the 5,000m swim race, building confidence in sustained continuous swimming at race pace is more valuable than short fast intervals; the 3×500m format bridges current 2km open-water sessions toward race distance.

proposed_changes.proposed_session: Easy endurance spin 45–50 min @ 120–145W (Z2), flat, HR ≤135 bpm — no intensity whatsoever
proposed_changes.reason: Threshold cycling intervals 9 days before the Half Oceanman generate fatigue that cannot be cleared in time and provide no meaningful swim-specific benefit; replacing with easy spinning maintains bike feel without cost.

proposed_changes.reason: A 4-hour 120km ride 7 days before the Half Oceanman is the highest single load in the pre-race week and would leave the athlete carrying significant fatigue into race day; a shorter capped ride maintains aerobic stimulus without the recovery cost.

proposed_changes.reason: A 21km long run 6 days before the Half Oceanman swim race is excessive and would leave the athlete arriving at the start line with unrecovered legs; a short easy jog keeps the routine without adding fatigue.

proposed_changes.reason: The day after the Half Oceanman 5,000m swim race the athlete will need active recovery, not a 21.5km long run; a short easy jog aids blood flow and keeps the Treviso 10K taper on track without adding stress 6 days before the run race.
